## Describing what happens precisely {.statement-slide}

Before we can ask how often something happens, we must say what counts as one thing happening.

Probability gives us a language for making both parts precise.

## Three questions organize this module {.compact}

1. **August 31:** What does one linguistic observation represent?
2. **September 2:** Which outcomes and events does our model distinguish?
3. **September 9:** How do probabilities change when we restrict attention to an event?

Each question begins with an intuition, adds a definition, and ends with a worked linguistic instance.

## The notes carry the full argument

Use these slides to see the sequence of questions and calculations. Use the [module notes](../../foundations/index.html) for the full explanations, linked readings, and practice questions.

We will return to the notes after each conceptual hinge rather than waiting until the end.

## A number is not yet an analysis {.statement-slide}

A reading time of 455 milliseconds is a measurement. It becomes evidence only after we say what was timed, under which linguistic condition, and for which population.

## Begin with the entity represented by one row

A recording can contain many word tokens, and several recordings can contribute to one speaker summary.

Thus a file, a row, and a linguistic observation need not be the same thing.

## Observational unit

**Definition** The [**observational unit**](../../foundations/linguistic-data.html) is the entity or event represented by one observation in the analysis.

One recording may contain many word-token observations. One speaker-level observation may combine several recordings.

## A worked unit specification

Suppose a participant reads several sentence regions.

> One observation represents one participant's reading of one region in one sentence.

The participant, sentence, and region identifiers together distinguish the observations.

## The unit determines what can vary {.statement-slide}

If we average over participants first, participant variation is no longer present in the analysis table.

[Continue in the notes: records, units, keys, tokens, and types](../../foundations/linguistic-data.html)

## Next ask what was recorded

A unit tells us what one observation represents. It does not yet say which property of that unit we recorded.

## Variables

**Definition** A **variable** assigns a value to each observational unit.

A vowel-token unit may have duration and formant-frequency estimates. A sentence-reading unit may have a reading-time variable and condition labels.

The value is not the unit: 455 milliseconds is a value assigned to a particular participant-by-sentence observation.

## A formant reflects an acoustic resonance

A [**formant**](https://www.fon.hum.uva.nl/praat/manual/Formant.html) is a concentration of acoustic energy associated with a vocal-tract resonance. A **formant-frequency estimate** records the estimated center frequency of that resonance in hertz, or cycles per second.

Thus a vowel token is the observational unit, while its first-formant frequency estimate is one value measured on that unit.

## Measurements and annotations answer different questions

**Definition** A **measurement** is a value produced by a stated recording procedure. An **annotation** is a label assigned under stated coding guidelines.

A reading time is a behavioral measurement. `Case=Acc` is an annotation assigned to a contextualized pronoun token.

Both may be variables, but neither should be mistaken for the linguistic token itself.

## Response and predictor are analytical roles

**Definition** The **response** is the variable whose variation the analysis aims to describe. A **predictor** is a variable used to describe or predict variation in the response.

Reading time may be the response, while coercion versus control condition is one possible predictor. A predictor may instead be continuous or derived. These names describe roles in an analysis, not fixed properties of a column.

## Next ask what the claim ranges over

One thousand tokens from one speaker may precisely describe that speaker. They do not measure variation across speakers.

## Target population and sample

**Definition** The target population is the collection of units to which the intended claim applies. The sample is the collection of units observed in the study.

The target population must be named. More observations from one speaker do not create observations from additional speakers.

## Finally state the quantity to be learned

“Does coercion matter?” does not yet name a numerical target. We must say which response, comparison, and population make the question testable.

The target might be the average response difference we would obtain across the population represented by the study.

## Estimand

**Definition** An [**estimand**](../../foundations/making-sense-of-data.html) is the population quantity that an analysis is intended to estimate.

For a two-condition study, one possible estimand is the difference between the two population means. The response, conditions, and population must be specified before that difference is interpretable.

## A processing example

An aspectual verb describes the start, continuation, or end of an event; *begin*, for instance, marks its start. A noun phrase such as *the book* ordinarily names an entity rather than an event.

In *began the book*, comprehenders may recover an unspoken event such as reading or writing the book. This configuration is called [**complement coercion**](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11062325/).

## How the processing response is measured

In **self-paced reading**, a participant reveals a sentence one predefined region at a time. The elapsed time before advancing provides a reading-time measurement for that region.

One estimand is the population mean difference in reading time over a predeclared region between coercion and matched noncoercing conditions.

## What the comparison holds fixed

Here **matched** means that the conditions are designed to differ in the need to recover an event while remaining similar in other relevant respects.

The comparison thus targets coercion more directly than a contrast between unrelated sentences would.

## The comparison-alignment problem {.statement-slide}

The unit, response, linguistic contrast, comparison, population, and estimand must describe the same question.

[Work through the coercion example in the notes](../../foundations/making-sense-of-data.html)

## Probability and statistics

Probability starts with a probability model and derives properties of possible observations.

Statistics starts with observed data and uses a model to estimate unknown population quantities or predict unobserved outcomes.

Using a sample to learn about a target population is **statistical inference**. This module first builds the probability language that inference requires.

## The course studies distinct data structures {.small}

| data structure | one possible observational unit | one possible response |
|---|---|---|
| corpus, a collection of language records | construction token | construction choice |
| experiment | participant by item trial | reading time or judgment |
| acoustic study of the speech signal | vowel token | duration or formant-frequency estimate |
| typological database of cross-language features | language by feature | coded feature value |

The analysis must retain every identifier needed to represent repeated speakers, items, words, languages, or documents.

## The first recurring check {.statement-slide}

Finish this sentence before calculating:

> One observation represents ______.

Then state what was measured or annotated on that observation.

## Six questions organize the course

::: {.incremental}
1. What can happen under the representation?
2. How can a variable describe those possibilities?
3. How does a probability distribution allocate probability across the variable's possible values?
4. What can a sample tell us about a larger population?
5. How does a model connect a linguistic predictor to a response?
6. How do we check the resulting description?
:::

## Describing an entire corpus {.section-slide}

<span class="section-subtitle">August 31</span>

## The linguistic question

How does frequency change as we move from common word forms to rare ones in one represented corpus?

To answer, we must decide what counts as a token, what counts as the same type, and how tied counts receive ranks.

## First distinguish occurrences from groups

The string *the* occurs 13 times in the represented address. Those are 13 occurrences grouped under one spelling.

Calling both things a “word” hides the distinction needed for counting.

## Token and type

**Definition** A [**token**](../../foundations/linguistic-data.html#tokens-and-types) is an occurrence in a particular context. A **type** groups tokens that the analysis treats as equivalent.

In this example, the **orthographic form** is the written string. The word-form type *the* groups 13 lowercased written tokens. A lemma-based analysis would use a different grouping rule.

## The observational unit is a word-form type

In the Washington address example, tokenization yields 135 word tokens assigned to 90 word types.

One row of the rank-frequency table represents one orthographic word-form type, not one token or lemma.

The source text is the 1793 address in quanteda's [US presidential inaugural corpus](https://quanteda.io/reference/data_corpus_inaugural.html).

## The grouping rule is part of the analysis

**Tokenization** applies a stated rule to divide the text into represented token occurrences. A **word-form type** groups tokens with the same represented form.

A **lemma** groups inflectionally related forms under a dictionary headword. Grouping *run*, *runs*, *ran*, and *running* under the lemma *run* would change the counts and ranks.

## A prediction before the formula

If a small number of types account for many tokens, frequency should fall quickly as we move down the ranked list.

An inverse-rank relation makes that qualitative prediction precise.

## Frequency and rank

For each type, frequency is its token count. Rank is assigned after sorting those counts from largest to smallest under a stated rule for ties.

Rank is thus derived from frequency; it is not a second independently observed measurement.

## Zipf's law names the comparison

**Definition** [**Zipf's law for word frequencies**](https://doi.org/10.3758/s13423-014-0585-6) is the approximate inverse relation between a represented type's frequency and its frequency rank.

It is a claim about a tokenization, type definition, corpus, and ranking rule. It is not a claim about unrepresented “words in English.”

## Defining rank-frequency notation

Let

$$
f(r)\equiv\text{token count of the type assigned rank }r.
$$

A common quantitative version specifies

$$
\widehat f(r)\equiv Cr^{-\alpha},
\qquad C>0,\ \alpha>0.
$$

Here $C$ sets the overall scale, while $\alpha$ controls how quickly predicted frequency falls as rank rises.

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

Piantadosi, Zipf's word frequency law in natural language: https://doi.org/10.3758/s13423-014-0585-6
:::

## What the parameters control

A **parameter** is a number that controls a model's predictions. Here $C$ sets the height of the curve and $\alpha$ controls how quickly it falls.

In contrast, $r$ is a type's derived rank and $\widehat f(r)$ is the model prediction at that rank.

## An inverse-rank calculation

For the illustrative choice $\alpha=1$ and $C=f(1)=13$,

$$
\widehat f(2)=6.5,
\qquad
\widehat f(3)\approx4.33,
\qquad
\widehat f(4)=3.25.
$$

These are model predictions, not observed counts.

## Compare each prediction with what occurred

The model predicts 6.5 tokens at rank 2. The observed type *of* has 11 tokens.

**Definition** A **residual** is an observed value minus the corresponding model prediction. Here the residual is $11-6.5=4.5$ tokens.

## Observed and predicted counts {.small}

| rank | observed $f(r)$ | predicted $\widehat f(r)$ | residual |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 13 | 13.00 | 0.00 |
| 2 | 11 | 6.50 | 4.50 |
| 3 | 6 | 4.33 | 1.67 |
| 4 | 5 | 3.25 | 1.75 |

The residual is defined by $e(r)\equiv f(r)-\widehat f(r)$.

## Logarithmic axes preserve multiplicative comparisons

Many types occur once, while a few occur thousands of times. An ordinary axis can crowd the rare types together.

**Definition** On a **logarithmic axis**, equal distances represent equal ratios: 1 to 10 occupies the same distance as 10 to 100. The transformation changes the display, not the observed ranks or counts.

## What should the plot show?

The broad inverse relation predicts a downward trend on ordinary axes and an approximately linear trend on logarithmic axes.

But the individual types need not lie exactly on one curve.

## The broad rank-frequency relation {.figure-slide}

![](figures/piantadosi-figure-1a.svg){width="53%" fig-alt="Normalized word frequency plotted against frequency rank for words in the American National Corpus."}

The red **Zipf-Mandelbrot curve** extends the basic inverse-rank curve with a rank shift. It is **fitted**, meaning that its parameter values were chosen to describe the observed points.

The gray **local average** smooths neighboring observations without imposing one global curve.

<span class="source">Piantadosi 2014, Figure 1a</span>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

https://doi.org/10.3758/s13423-014-0585-6
:::

## Residuals show what the curve omits {.figure-slide}

![](figures/piantadosi-figure-1b.svg){width="53%" fig-alt="Difference between observed log word frequency and the Zipf-Mandelbrot prediction, plotted against log frequency rank."}

Long runs above and below zero show systematic departures from the fitted curve.

<span class="source">Piantadosi 2014, Figure 1b</span>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

https://doi.org/10.3758/s13423-014-0585-6
:::

## The fitted relation is descriptive

A close fit licenses a claim about the relation between type frequency and derived rank in the represented corpus.

It does not identify the process that generated the token sequence.

## The description-explanation gap {.statement-slide}

Matching the broad curve tells us that a model describes the rank-frequency relation.

It does not tell us why speakers produced those tokens in that order.

## One curve can follow from incompatible processes

Independent character generation with occasional boundaries can produce an approximately Zipfian rank-frequency pattern for strings.

Human word production does not satisfy that character-generation model.

## False boundaries preserve the broad relation {.figure-slide}

![](figures/piantadosi-figure-9.svg){width="43%" fig-alt="Frequency distribution of strings created by treating the letter e as a word boundary in the American National Corpus."}

An approximate rank-frequency fit can survive a segmentation rule that does not recover words.

<span class="source">Piantadosi 2014, Figure 9</span>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

https://doi.org/10.3758/s13423-014-0585-6
:::

## The result updates the question

The broad curve survives a segmentation rule that does not recover words.

Thus the interesting linguistic question is not merely whether a mechanism produces a Zipfian curve. It is which additional predictions distinguish that mechanism from incompatible alternatives.

## The example separates three objects {.compact}

1. **Data:** token counts under a stated tokenization and type definition
2. **Derived ordering:** frequency rank under a stated tie rule
3. **Model:** predicted frequency as a function of rank

A process explanation requires additional predictions that distinguish competing mechanisms.

## August 31: analysis specification {.compact}

1. State what one observation represents.
2. State how the response is measured.
3. State how any derived predictor is constructed.
4. Separate descriptive fit from evidence about the process that produced the data.

## Probability spaces {.section-slide}

<span class="section-subtitle">September 2</span>

## The question for September 2

What must a model represent before it can assign a probability to a linguistic event?

We will specify possible token records, the events we can ask about, and the probability assigned to each event.

## The random experiment

Select one contextualized personal-pronoun token from a specified corpus population and inspect its annotated record.

The **corpus population** is the declared collection of token records eligible for selection. Each record contains at least an orthographic form and the annotation values `Person`, `Number`, and `Case`.

**Definition** A **random experiment** is a repeatable procedure whose represented result is not known before one run of the procedure occurs.

## Token, form, and annotation are different objects

Consider *They saw you*.

1. The occurrence of *you* at a particular corpus position is a **token**.
2. `you` is its orthographic **form**.
3. `Case=Acc` is an **annotation value** assigned using the token's syntactic context.

[Universal Dependencies' English Case guidelines](https://universaldependencies.org/en/feat/Case.html) treat *you* and *it* as compatible with both `Nom` and `Acc`.

## The annotation scheme used here

`Person=3` marks reference outside the speaker-addressee pair. `Number=Sing/Plur` records whether the form belongs to the scheme's singular or plural category; the label need not transparently count discourse referents.

For this toy example, `Case=Nom` labels pronoun forms in subject contexts and `Case=Acc` labels forms in object or prepositional contexts, following the linked UD scheme. The labels do not directly encode who did what to whom.

## One possible result

Suppose the selected token record is

$$
\langle\text{FORM=them},\text{Person=3},\text{Number=Plur},\text{Case=Acc}\rangle.
$$

This whole record is one possible result. `them`, `Plur`, and `Acc` are three values recorded on that result.

## Outcome and sample space

**Definition** An [**outcome**](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html) is one possible result. The [**sample space**](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html) is the set of all outcomes, denoted by $\Omega$.

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html
:::

## A form-only representation {.small}

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Omega_{\mathrm{form}}\equiv\{&\textit{I},\textit{me},\textit{you},\textit{they},
\textit{them},\textit{it},\textit{she},\textit{her},\\
&\textit{he},\textit{him},\textit{we},\textit{us}\}.
\end{aligned}
$$

This representation retains only the orthographic form category. It drops contextual distinctions present in the token record.

## Predict the limitation

If the outcome records only form, can the model ask whether the token was annotated `Case=Nom` or `Case=Acc`?

Compare *You left* with *I saw you*. The written form is *you* in both contexts, but the linked annotation scheme assigns `Nom` in the first and `Acc` in the second.

## Syncretism

**Definition** A [**syncretic form**](https://universaldependencies.org/en/feat/Case.html) is one form associated with more than one grammatical annotation value.

Thus the orthographic form *you* alone does not determine its case annotation. Context is required.

## A reduced sample space for later calculations

For later calculations, restrict attention to four fully annotated third-person record categories:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Omega_4\equiv\{&\langle\textit{he},\mathrm{Sing},\mathrm{Nom}\rangle,
\langle\textit{him},\mathrm{Sing},\mathrm{Acc}\rangle,\\
&\langle\textit{they},\mathrm{Plur},\mathrm{Nom}\rangle,
\langle\textit{them},\mathrm{Plur},\mathrm{Acc}\rangle\}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Each run produces exactly one represented record category. We abbreviate these categories by their forms when no confusion can arise.

## The sample space is part of the model

$\langle\textit{herself},\ldots\rangle\notin\Omega_4$ means that the reduced model does not represent a *herself* record as a possible result.

It makes no claim about what English speakers can produce outside this experiment.

## The representation fixes the available questions {.statement-slide}

A form-only outcome can answer a form question. A case question requires contextual information or an explicit case annotation.

[Continue in the notes: sample spaces and outcome granularity](../../foundations/possibilities-and-events.html)

## Set-theoretic notation {.compact}

This module uses the set theory reviewed in [*Languages as formal objects*](https://aaronstevenwhite.io/intro-to-cl/languages-as-formal-objects/).

1. $x\in B$: outcome $x$ belongs to set $B$
2. $B\cap C$: outcomes in both sets
3. $B\cup C$: outcomes in at least one set
4. $B^c$: outcomes in $\Omega$ but not in $B$
5. $\varnothing$: the event containing no outcomes

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

https://aaronstevenwhite.io/intro-to-cl/languages-as-formal-objects/
:::

## An event is a yes-or-no question

After one token record is selected, we can ask: is its `Number` value `Plur`? Is its `Case` value `Acc`?

Each question collects the outcomes for which the answer is yes.

## Events

**Definition** An [**event**](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html) is a subset of $\Omega$. The event occurs when the realized outcome belongs to that subset.

An event is not a second outcome. It groups the outcomes that give the same answer to a question.

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html
:::

## Number and case events in the reduced space

For $\Omega_4$, define

$$
P_4\equiv\{\textit{they},\textit{them}\}
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
A_4\equiv\{\textit{him},\textit{them}\}.
$$

$P_4$ is the plural event. $A_4$ is the accusative event.

These are events about annotation values. The italicized forms merely abbreviate the fully annotated record categories in $\Omega_4$.

## From a recorded value back to outcomes

A **map** is a rule that assigns each outcome one value. Let $N$ map each outcome to its `Number` value, so $N(\omega)$ is one value such as `Plur`.

The plural event instead collects every outcome mapped to that value.

## Preimage

**Definition** The [**preimage**](../../random-variables-and-distributions/defining-random-variables.html) of a value set contains every outcome that the map sends into that set.

For plurality,

$$
P_4=N^{-1}(\{\mathrm{Plur}\})=\{\textit{they},\textit{them}\}.
$$

The preimage is an event in the outcome space, not a value in the value space.

## Why preimages matter {.statement-slide}

Probability measures assign probabilities to events. A preimage lets us ask for the probability of a recorded value by identifying the outcomes that produce it.

Module 2 develops this outcome-to-value map as a random variable.

## Intersections encode conjunction

$$
P_4\cap A_4=\{\textit{them}\}.
$$

The event $P_4\cap A_4$ occurs exactly when the selected record has `Number=Plur` and `Case=Acc`.

## Complements are relative to the sample space

$$
P_4^c=\{\textit{he},\textit{him}\}.
$$

This complement is taken relative to $\Omega_4$.

## Which event questions belong in one model?

If a model can ask whether a token is plural, it must also represent “not plural.” If it can ask two questions, it must represent “at least one is true.”

The event space records a collection of questions that remains coherent under these operations.

## Sigma-algebra

**Definition** A [**sigma-algebra**](https://stats.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Probability_Theory/Probability_Mathematical_Statistics_and_Stochastic_Processes_%28Siegrist%29/01%3A_Foundations/1.11%3A_Measurable_Spaces) $\mathcal F$ is a collection of subsets of $\Omega$ that contains $\Omega$ and is closed under complements and countable unions.

Members of $\mathcal F$ are called **measurable events**. Here *measurable* means “included in the mathematical event space,” not “recorded by an instrument.”

## Closure keeps operations inside the event space

**Closed under complements** means that $B^c$ belongs to $\mathcal F$ whenever $B$ does.

**Closed under countable unions** means that the union of any list $B_1,B_2,\ldots$ also belongs to $\mathcal F$. The list may be finite or countably infinite.

## The three closure requirements {.compact}

$$
\Omega\in\mathcal F,
$$

$$
B\in\mathcal F\Longrightarrow B^c\in\mathcal F,
$$

$$
B_1,B_2,\ldots\in\mathcal F
\Longrightarrow \bigcup_{i=1}^{\infty}B_i\in\mathcal F.
$$

The empty event $\varnothing$ and intersections follow from these requirements.

## A sigma-algebra for number only

If the model distinguishes only plurality, then

$$
\mathcal F_{P_4}\equiv\{\varnothing,P_4,P_4^c,\Omega_4\}.
$$

The accusative event $A_4$ is not measurable because $A_4\notin\mathcal F_{P_4}$.

This is a limit of the represented event space, not evidence that corpus case annotation is impossible.

## Two small event spaces do not combine by union

Let $\mathcal F_{A_4}=\{\varnothing,A_4,A_4^c,\Omega_4\}$. The set $\mathcal F_{P_4}\cup\mathcal F_{A_4}$ contains both $P_4$ and $A_4$ but not their intersection $P_4\cap A_4$.

Thus this union is not closed under intersections and is not a sigma-algebra.

## We need the smallest coherent expansion

Start with the questions “plural?” and “accusative?” Then add every complement, union, and intersection required by the sigma-algebra rules.

The result is the event space generated by $P_4$ and $A_4$.

## Generated sigma-algebra

**Definition** $\sigma(P_4,A_4)$ denotes the smallest sigma-algebra containing $P_4$ and $A_4$. The set $\{P_4,A_4\}$ is a [**generating set**](https://stats.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Probability_Theory/Probability_Mathematical_Statistics_and_Stochastic_Processes_%28Siegrist%29/01%3A_Foundations/1.11%3A_Measurable_Spaces).

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

https://stats.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Probability_Theory/Probability_Mathematical_Statistics_and_Stochastic_Processes_%28Siegrist%29/01%3A_Foundations/1.11%3A_Measurable_Spaces
:::

## Atoms are the finest cells left by the questions

**Definition** An **atom** is a nonempty measurable event that contains no smaller nonempty measurable event.

With two yes-or-no questions, an outcome must fall into one of four cells: yes-yes, yes-no, no-yes, or no-no.

## Atoms of $\sigma(P_4,A_4)$ {.compact}

The nonempty intersections are

$$
P_4\cap A_4=\{\textit{them}\},\qquad
P_4\cap A_4^c=\{\textit{they}\},
$$

$$
P_4^c\cap A_4=\{\textit{him}\},\qquad
P_4^c\cap A_4^c=\{\textit{he}\}.
$$

## The atoms determine the event space

Each atom contains one outcome and is thus a **singleton**. Every subset of $\Omega_4$ is a union of these four atoms. Thus

$$
\sigma(P_4,A_4)=2^{\Omega_4}.
$$

The notation $2^{\Omega_4}$ denotes the **power set**, the collection of every subset of $\Omega_4$.

## What the event space buys us {.statement-slide}

Once $\mathcal F$ contains the questions we care about, one probability measure can assign probabilities to all of them consistently.

[See the full construction in the sigma-algebra notes](../../foundations/event-spaces.html) and [the generated-space notes](../../foundations/generating-event-spaces.html).

## A probability measure assigns coherent weights

We want “How likely is the accusative event?” to return one number between zero and one, and we want probabilities of disjoint alternatives to add.

That job belongs to the probability measure.

## Probability measure

**Definition** A [**probability measure**](https://stats.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Probability_Theory/Probability_Mathematical_Statistics_and_Stochastic_Processes_%28Siegrist%29/02%3A_Probability_Spaces/2.09%3A_Probability_Spaces_Revisited) is a function

$$
\mathbb{P}:\mathcal F\to[0,1]
$$

that satisfies the probability axioms.

The blackboard-bold symbol $\mathbb{P}$ is reserved for the probability measure; its arguments are events in $\mathcal F$.

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

https://stats.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Probability_Theory/Probability_Mathematical_Statistics_and_Stochastic_Processes_%28Siegrist%29/02%3A_Probability_Spaces/2.09%3A_Probability_Spaces_Revisited
:::

## Three rules prevent contradictory assignments

1. No event receives a negative probability.
2. The entire sample space receives probability one.
3. Probabilities add across events that share no outcomes.

These rules are the probability axioms.

## Probability axioms {.compact}

For every $B\in\mathcal F$,

$$
\mathbb{P}(B)\geq0,
\qquad
\mathbb{P}(\Omega)=1.
$$

For pairwise disjoint $B_1,B_2,\ldots\in\mathcal F$,

$$
\mathbb{P}\!\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^{\infty}B_i\right)
=\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\mathbb{P}(B_i).
$$

**Pairwise disjoint** means that no two events in the list share an outcome.

## Predict before calculating

Suppose the singular outcome categories receive probabilities $.20$ and $.30$, while the plural categories receive $.10$ and $.40$.

What probability should the model assign to the plural event? To the accusative event?

## Probability space

**Definition** The triple

$$
(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb{P})
$$

is a [**probability space**](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html).

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html
:::

The sample space states what can happen, the event space states which questions can be asked, and the probability measure assigns coherent weights to those questions.

## A probability measure on $\Omega_4$ {.small}

| outcome $\omega$ | $\mathbb{P}(\{\omega\})$ |
|---|---:|
| *he* | $.20$ |
| *him* | $.30$ |
| *they* | $.10$ |
| *them* | $.40$ |

The four one-outcome probabilities are nonnegative and sum to one.

## Probability of an event

Because the singleton events are disjoint,

$$
\mathbb{P}(A_4)
=\mathbb{P}(\{\textit{him}\})+\mathbb{P}(\{\textit{them}\})
=.30+.40=.70.
$$

Similarly, $\mathbb P(P_4)=.10+.40=.50$.

## Check the axioms

Consider a different proposed assignment in which the four one-outcome events together cover $\Omega_4$ and receive probabilities $.40$, $.35$, $.20$, and $.10$.

Their sum is $1.05$, so the assignment is not a probability measure.

## September 2: definitions {.compact}

1. $\Omega$ contains all possible outcomes.
2. $\mathcal F$ contains the measurable events.
3. $\mathbb{P}$ assigns probabilities to events in $\mathcal F$.
4. $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb{P})$ is the probability space.

## September 2: the linguistic upshot {.statement-slide}

The probability model does not discover whether an outcome is a token, form, lemma, or annotation category. We decide that representation first.

Module 2 will turn attributes of these outcomes into random variables.

## Read the probability-space notes

[Sample spaces](../../foundations/possibilities-and-events.html)

[Events](../../foundations/events.html)

[Sigma-algebras](../../foundations/event-spaces.html)

[Probability measures](../../foundations/probability-measures.html)

## Joint and conditional probability {.section-slide}

<span class="section-subtitle">September 9</span>

## The question for September 9

How much probability belongs to outcomes satisfying two linguistic descriptions, and how should probability change when one description is already known?

We begin with the same four annotated record categories.

## The fixed probability space {.small}

| outcome | number | case | probability |
|---|---|---|---:|
| *he* | singular | nominative | $.20$ |
| *him* | singular | accusative | $.30$ |
| *they* | plural | nominative | $.10$ |
| *them* | plural | accusative | $.40$ |

All calculations on September 9 use this probability space unless stated otherwise.

## First ask whether two events can co-occur

The singular and plural events cannot occur for the same outcome in $\Omega_4$.

The plural and accusative events can co-occur: *them* belongs to both.

## Mutually exclusive events

**Definition** Events $B$ and $C$ are [**mutually exclusive**](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html) if

$$
B\cap C=\varnothing.
$$

They cannot occur for the same selected outcome.

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html
:::

Plural and singular are mutually exclusive. Plural and accusative are not.

## Addition rule for disjoint events

If $B\cap C=\varnothing$, the third probability axiom gives

$$
\mathbb{P}(B\cup C)=\mathbb{P}(B)+\mathbb{P}(C).
$$

## Addition rule for arbitrary events

If $B$ and $C$ can overlap, subtract the overlap counted twice:

$$
\mathbb{P}(B\cup C)
=\mathbb{P}(B)+\mathbb{P}(C)-\mathbb{P}(B\cap C).
$$

## Joint probability asks for the overlap

For a selected token record, we may ask whether `Number=Plur` and `Case=Acc` both hold.

The answer concerns the intersection $P_4\cap A_4$, not two separate selections.

## Joint-probability notation

**Definition** For events $B,C\in\mathcal F$, define

$$
\mathbb{P}(B,C)\equiv\mathbb{P}(B\cap C).
$$

The comma means that both events occur.

## Joint probability of plurality and case

Because $P_4\cap A_4=\{\textit{them}\}$,

$$
\mathbb{P}(P_4,A_4)
=\mathbb{P}(\{\textit{them}\})
=.40.
$$

## The joint-probability table {.small}

| | accusative $A_4$ | nominative $A_4^c$ | total |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| plural $P_4$ | $\mathbb{P}(P_4,A_4)=.40$ | $\mathbb{P}(P_4,A_4^c)=.10$ | $.50$ |
| singular $P_4^c$ | $\mathbb{P}(P_4^c,A_4)=.30$ | $\mathbb{P}(P_4^c,A_4^c)=.20$ | $.50$ |
| total | $.70$ | $.30$ | $1$ |

## Recovering a row or column total

To recover the probability of plurality, add the two mutually exclusive ways a plural token can be coded for case: plural-accusative and plural-nominative.

**Definition** **Marginalization** sums over every represented alternative for one distinction to recover the probability for another distinction.

## Marginalization adds all case alternatives

The disjoint events $P_4\cap A_4$ and $P_4\cap A_4^c$ have union $P_4$. The third probability axiom thus gives

$$
\mathbb{P}(P_4)
=\mathbb{P}(P_4,A_4)+\mathbb{P}(P_4,A_4^c).
$$

## Marginalizing over case

Substitute the two cells in the plural row:

$$
\mathbb{P}(P_4)=.40+.10=.50.
$$

The alternatives $A_4$ and $A_4^c$ share no outcomes and together cover every represented case value. Thus their joint probabilities with $P_4$ add to $\mathbb{P}(P_4)$.

## The joint table answers two kinds of questions {.statement-slide}

A cell answers a conjunction question. A row or column total answers a marginal question after summing over the other annotation.

[Work through the table in the joint-probability notes](../../foundations/joint-probability-of-events.html)

## Conditioning changes the reference set

Suppose we already know that the token is plural. The relevant possibilities are now *they* and *them*, whose total probability is $.50$.

We ask what share of that restricted probability is accusative.

## Conditional-probability notation

$\mathbb{P}(B\mid C)$ is read as “the probability of $B$ given $C$.”

$B$ is the target event. $C$ is the conditioning event.

## Conditional probability

**Definition** If $\mathbb{P}(C)>0$, then

$$
\mathbb{P}(B\mid C)
\equiv\frac{\mathbb{P}(B,C)}{\mathbb{P}(C)}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html
:::

The definition rescales the probabilities within $C$ so that the restricted probabilities sum to one.

## The denominator defines the reference set

For $\mathbb{P}(A_4\mid P_4)$, first restrict to $P_4$. Then calculate the proportion of that probability that also belongs to $A_4$.

$$
\mathbb{P}(A_4\mid P_4)=\frac{\mathbb{P}(A_4,P_4)}{\mathbb{P}(P_4)}.
$$

## Conditional probability of accusative case

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(A_4\mid P_4)
&=\frac{\mathbb{P}(A_4,P_4)}{\mathbb{P}(P_4)}\\
&=\frac{.40}{.50}\\
&=.80.
\end{aligned}
$$

## Reversing the condition

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(P_4\mid A_4)
&=\frac{\mathbb{P}(P_4,A_4)}{\mathbb{P}(A_4)}\\
&=\frac{.40}{.70}\\
&\approx.571.
\end{aligned}
$$

The numerator is unchanged. The denominator is not.

## Direction matters {.statement-slide}

Eighty percent of the plural probability is accusative, but about 57 percent of the accusative probability is plural.

Changing the condition changes the question. [See the conditioning diagrams and calculations in the notes](../../foundations/conditional-probability.html).

## Chain rule {.section-slide}

<span class="section-subtitle">Derivation from conditional probability</span>

## Reconstruct a conjunction from two pieces

We know that plural outcomes receive probability $.50$. Within that restricted probability, $.80$ is accusative.

Multiplying the restricted proportion by the probability of the restriction should recover the plural-accusative cell.

## Begin with the definition

For $\mathbb{P}(C)>0$,

$$
\mathbb{P}(B\mid C)
\equiv\frac{\mathbb{P}(B,C)}{\mathbb{P}(C)}.
$$

## Multiply by the denominator

Multiply both sides by $\mathbb{P}(C)$:

$$
\mathbb{P}(B\mid C)\mathbb{P}(C)
=\mathbb{P}(B,C).
$$

## Two-event chain rule

Reorder the equality:

$$
\boxed{\mathbb{P}(B,C)
=\mathbb{P}(B\mid C)\mathbb{P}(C)}.
$$

**Definition** The **chain rule**, also called the [**multiplication rule**](https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat414/Lesson04), rewrites a joint probability as the probability of one event times the conditional probability of the other.

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat414/Lesson04
:::

## Chain-rule calculation

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(A_4,P_4)
&=\mathbb{P}(A_4\mid P_4)\mathbb{P}(P_4)\\
&=.80(.50)\\
&=.40.
\end{aligned}
$$

The conditional proportion $.80$ applies within the probability $.50$ assigned to $P_4$.

Thus $.80(.50)=.40$ reconstructs the joint probability.

## Three-event chain rule

Suppose $\mathbb{P}(B)>0$ and $\mathbb{P}(B,C)>0$. First separate the final event from the first two:

$$
\mathbb{P}(B,C,D)
=\mathbb{P}(D\mid B,C)\mathbb{P}(B,C).
$$

## Factor the remaining joint probability

Apply the two-event rule again:

$$
\mathbb{P}(B,C)=\mathbb{P}(C\mid B)\mathbb{P}(B).
$$

Substitution gives

$$
\boxed{\mathbb{P}(B,C,D)
=\mathbb{P}(B)\mathbb{P}(C\mid B)\mathbb{P}(D\mid B,C)}.
$$

## The chain rule does not assume independence {.statement-slide}

Each factor may depend on the events that precede it in the chosen ordering. Independence permits a conditional factor to be replaced by a marginal factor.

A **factorization** is such a rewriting of one joint probability as a product of simpler probability terms.

[Derive both orderings in the chain-rule notes](../../foundations/probability-factorization.html)

## Bayes' rule {.section-slide}

<span class="section-subtitle">Reverse the conditioning direction</span>

## The direction-reversal question

Suppose slow reading is common in a coercion condition. Among all slow trials, how many came from that condition?

The first probability conditions on the experimental condition. The second conditions on the observed response category.

## Factor the same joint probability twice

$$
\mathbb{P}(B,C)=\mathbb{P}(B\mid C)\mathbb{P}(C)
$$

and

$$
\mathbb{P}(B,C)=\mathbb{P}(C\mid B)\mathbb{P}(B).
$$

## Equate the factorizations

Because both right sides equal $\mathbb{P}(B,C)$,

$$
\mathbb{P}(B\mid C)\mathbb{P}(C)
=\mathbb{P}(C\mid B)\mathbb{P}(B).
$$

## Derive Bayes' rule

If $\mathbb{P}(C)>0$, divide by $\mathbb{P}(C)$:

$$
\boxed{\mathbb{P}(B\mid C)
=\frac{\mathbb{P}(C\mid B)\mathbb{P}(B)}{\mathbb{P}(C)}}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html
:::

## Toy processing counts {.small}

| | slow event $S$ | not slow $S^c$ | total |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| coercion condition $C$ | 90 | 10 | 100 |
| control condition $C^c$ | 180 | 720 | 900 |
| total | 270 | 730 | 1,000 |

The random experiment selects one trial from this represented population. “Slow” means that reading time in a predeclared region exceeds a cutoff chosen before inspecting these counts; the counts are illustrative.

## Conditioning on the experimental condition

$$
\mathbb{P}(S\mid C)=\frac{90}{100}=.90.
$$

This denominator contains only coercion trials.

## Conditioning on the observed response category

$$
\mathbb{P}(C\mid S)=\frac{90}{270}=\frac13.
$$

This denominator contains all trials classified as slow.

## Bayes' rule calculation

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(C\mid S)
&=\frac{\mathbb{P}(S\mid C)\mathbb{P}(C)}{\mathbb{P}(S)}\\
&=\frac{.90(.10)}{.27}\\
&=\frac13.
\end{aligned}
$$

## Bayes' rule does not identify a mechanism {.statement-slide}

The calculation reverses a conditional probability under the stated joint distribution. It does not show that coercion caused a trial to cross the threshold.

[Work through the same direction reversal in the Bayes' rule notes](../../foundations/bayes-rule.html). The linguistic motivation comes from [reading-time work on complement coercion](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11062325/).

## Independence {.section-slide}

<span class="section-subtitle">Conditioning provides no information</span>

## Ask whether the restriction changes anything

If knowing that a token is plural leaves the probability of accusative case unchanged, number provides no probabilistic information about case under this measure.

That invariance is the intuition behind independence.

## Independence as invariance under conditioning

If $\mathbb{P}(C)>0$, conditioning on $C$ leaves the probability of $B$ unchanged exactly when

$$
\mathbb{P}(B\mid C)=\mathbb{P}(B).
$$

This equality is one way to state independence.

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat414/Lesson05
:::

Because no third event is held fixed here, this relation is also called **marginal independence**. Module 2 will contrast it with conditional independence.

## Plurality and case are dependent

$$
\mathbb{P}(A_4\mid P_4)=.80
\qquad\text{but}\qquad
\mathbb{P}(A_4)=.70.
$$

Thus the conditional and marginal probabilities differ. Plurality and case are dependent under this probability measure.

## Derive the product test for independence

Start from the chain rule:

$$
\mathbb{P}(B,C)=\mathbb{P}(B\mid C)\mathbb{P}(C).
$$

Under independence, substitute $\mathbb{P}(B)$ for $\mathbb{P}(B\mid C)$.

## The definition valid for all events

**Definition** Events $B$ and $C$ are independent, written $B\perp\!\!\!\perp C$, exactly when

$$
\boxed{
B\perp\!\!\!\perp C
\quad\equiv\quad
\bigl[\mathbb{P}(B,C)=\mathbb{P}(B)\mathbb{P}(C)\bigr]
}.
$$

When $\mathbb P(C)>0$, this definition is equivalent to $\mathbb P(B\mid C)=\mathbb P(B)$.

## Check the pronoun joint probability

$$
\mathbb{P}(P_4,A_4)=.40
$$

but

$$
\mathbb{P}(P_4)\mathbb{P}(A_4)=.50(.70)=.35.
$$

The factorization fails, as the conditional comparison already showed.

## An independent comparison {.small}

| | accusative $A_4$ | nominative $A_4^c$ | total |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| plural $P_4$ | $.35$ | $.15$ | $.50$ |
| singular $P_4^c$ | $.35$ | $.15$ | $.50$ |
| total | $.70$ | $.30$ | $1$ |

Here $\mathbb{P}(A_4\mid P_4)=.35/.50=.70=\mathbb{P}(A_4)$.

## Mutual exclusivity is not independence

If $B\cap C=\varnothing$ and $\mathbb{P}(B),\mathbb{P}(C)>0$, then

$$
\mathbb{P}(B\mid C)=0\neq\mathbb{P}(B).
$$

Observing $C$ rules out $B$.

## Independence is a property of the measure {.statement-slide}

The same number and case events can be independent under one probability measure and dependent under another.

It is not a claim that the linguistic annotations have no relationship in every corpus or population. [Compare the two measures in the independence notes](../../foundations/independence.html).

## Module summary {.section-slide}

<span class="section-subtitle">Represent first, then calculate</span>

## The three hinges

1. A linguistic record becomes data only after the unit, measurement or annotation, comparison, and target are specified.
2. A probability space represents outcomes, answerable event questions, and their probabilities.
3. Joint, conditional, and independence statements are properties of that declared representation and measure.

## Probability-space notation {.compact}

1. $\Omega$: possible outcomes
2. $\mathcal F$: measurable events
3. $\mathbb{P}$: probability measure on $\mathcal F$
4. $\mathbb{P}(B,C)\equiv\mathbb{P}(B\cap C)$: joint probability
5. $\mathbb{P}(B\mid C)$: conditional probability

## Conditional probability and its consequences {.compact}

$$
\mathbb{P}(B\mid C)\equiv\frac{\mathbb{P}(B,C)}{\mathbb{P}(C)}
$$

$$
\mathbb{P}(B,C)=\mathbb{P}(B\mid C)\mathbb{P}(C)
$$

$$
\mathbb{P}(B\mid C)=\frac{\mathbb{P}(C\mid B)\mathbb{P}(B)}{\mathbb{P}(C)}
$$

## Independence {.compact}

$$
B\perp\!\!\!\perp C
\quad\equiv\quad
\bigl[\mathbb{P}(B,C)=\mathbb{P}(B)\mathbb{P}(C)\bigr].
$$

If $\mathbb P(C)>0$, equivalently $\mathbb P(B\mid C)=\mathbb P(B)$.

## What Module 2 may now assume {.statement-slide}

You can distinguish an outcome from a recorded value, identify an event as a subset of outcomes, condition on a positive-probability event, and test independence without holding a third event fixed.

Next, we use random variables to map token outcomes to form, annotation, count, and measurement values.
